item.title: PM discusses Middle East tensions, safety of Bangladeshi workers with Iran President
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and discussed the Middle East conflict and the safety of Bangladeshi workers, while seeking Iran’s cooperation in facilitating the movement of Bangladeshi vessels and containers through the Strait of Hormuz.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and Prime Minister’s Adviser Mahdi Amin briefed journalists on the meeting at a press briefing later in the day at the Hyatt Grand Central New York hotel.
Kobir said the Prime Minister called for an early resolution of the conflict through diplomacy, stressing its potential impact on Bangladesh, particularly on Bangladeshi expatriate workers and the country’s energy security.
Bangladesh has a significant number of workers and professionals in the Middle East, and any prolonged conflict in the region could have an impact on the country, he said.
The state minister also said Bangladesh raised the issue of containers and vessels being held up amid the tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and sought Iran’s cooperation in facilitating their safe movement once the situation improves.
“We called for a quick resolution through diplomacy,” he said, adding that the Iranian President listened to Bangladesh’s concerns and took note of them.
Kobir said Bangladesh maintains a neutral position and is prepared to play a constructive role in promoting peace and stability if there is an opportunity.
“Bangladesh can become a soft-medium influence for good, for peace and stability in the world,” he said.
The state minister said Bangladesh has important partners across the Middle East, and some of them have encouraged Bangladesh to use its neutral position to communicate with parties involved in the conflict.
He said Bangladesh does not necessarily need to take a visible mediation role, but can engage as a friend of the region and contribute to peace and stability through diplomatic channels.
“The UN is a neutral venue,” Kobir said, referring to the meeting with the Iranian President at the UN Headquarters.
He said the Prime Minister used the opportunity to discuss both the conflict and Bangladesh’s national interests, including the possible impact of the situation around the Strait of Hormuz on the country’s energy supply and trade.
The state minister said Bangladesh wants an early and peaceful resolution to the conflict through diplomacy, as a prolonged crisis could have wider regional and international consequences.
Mahdi said the meeting also focused on regional stability, the safety of Bangladeshi workers in the broader Middle East and issues related to regional and international peace.
He said the prime minister emphasised Bangladesh’s national interests, particularly the safety and well-being of its expatriate population.
The meeting took place as part of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s engagements on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly.

item.title: 624 detained in simultaneous Comilla police raids
item.description:
Police detained 624 people in Comilla for questioning over alleged involvement in criminal activities during a coordinated drive across all 18 police stations in the district on Wednesday night.
Lutfur Rahman, additional superintendent of police and media officer of Comilla District Police, said the detainees were being questioned and that legal action would follow after police verified the information gathered.
He said the recent involvement of adolescents in various criminal activities has been having a negative impact on society.
Following the directives of Superintendent of Police Anisuzzaman, simultaneous raids were conducted across the district, targeting areas known for harassment and disorderly activities by youths, including various locations in Comilla city and areas under the respective police stations.
Senior district police officials also took part in the operation, Lutfur said.
He said necessary legal action would be taken after verifying the detainees’ previous involvement in criminal activities.
District police plan to conduct such drives regularly to prevent adolescents from becoming involved in crime, he added.
Concerns over the activities of “teen gangs” in Comilla resurfaced following the murder of 13-year-old Opratim, son of Comilla University teacher Nahida Begum. Police launched a major operation following the incident.
Meanwhile, 17 detainees allegedly escaped from a holding room at Daudkandi police station on Wednesday night after breaking down the door.
Lutfur said the incident occurred because the room had become overcrowded. Locals later caught the escapees and brought them back to the police station.
He said the incident took place amid a gathering of people at the station who had come to inquire about the mass detentions.

item.title: UNGA President Khailur urges sustained global focus on Rohingya crisis
item.description:
President of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) Dr Khalilur Rahman has expressed concern that familiar patterns of violence and persecution continue to cast a long shadow across Rakhine state and the rest of Myanmar, noting that the Rohingya crisis is not over.
The assembly president underscored the importance of sustained political attention to keep the Rohingya crisis high on the international agenda.
Predictable humanitarian assistance, he said, would also remain critical.
At a high-level side event on the Rohingya crisis in New York on Wednesday, he joined discussions highlighting the urgency of achieving durable solutions to protracted displacement, including through conditions for safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return.
After years of displacement, the UNGA president said the international community must not allow attention to fade.
"We must sustain political attention, support refugees and host communities, pursue accountability and ensure that the Rohingya themselves have a meaningful voice in shaping the conditions for their safe return home," he said.
Describing the situation in Myanmar, Dr Rahman said civilians face indiscriminate attacks, air strikes, arbitrary arrest and detention, torture, enforced disappearances, forced recruitment, destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure, and the denial of humanitarian assistance.
Nine years after the mass displacement of the Rohingya from Myanmar, their situation remains one of the world's most protracted and complex refugee crises, marked by years of persecution and uncertainty over the prospect of returning home.
Against this backdrop, senior UN officials renewed calls for a durable solution that would enable Rohingya refugees to return home safely and with dignity, while ensuring justice and accountability.
UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a keynote speaker at a high-level event held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the General Assembly, reminded participants that nearly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh.
“An entire generation is growing up in exile…Conflicts continue in Myanmar. Conditions for voluntary, safe, and dignified, and sustainable return do not exist at the moment.”
In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched a crackdown in the country's western Rakhine state, forcing hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims to flee across the border into Bangladesh, where the vast majority remain refugees, according to the United Nations.
The Secretary-General's Special Envoy on Myanmar, Julie Bishop, lamented that for children born in 2017, displacement now encompasses their entire childhood.
“It's estimated that over 30,000 children are born into the camp each year.”
The envoy said women and girls living in the camps face growing risks of gender-based violence, including from armed groups and criminal networks, while access to protection services is declining. "The young are losing hope."
UN officials commended Bangladesh for its extraordinary hospitality and generosity but cautioned that the international community cannot stand by while the country continues to host the world's largest refugee settlement.
“When funding disappears, needs do not disappear with it. There is less food, less education, fewer opportunities, greater pressure on health and other essential services, and more desperation for families,” the UNHCR chief said.
Without prospects for a safe and dignified future, Rohingya refugees face increasing risks of exploitation, trafficking, forced conscription and dangerous sea journeys.
In his address, Prime Minister of Bangladesh Tarique Rahman drew attention to the growing costs of prolonged displacement, both for the Rohingya and for host communities.
“Prolonged uncertainty and disruption are creating new challenges and security risks, including human trafficking, migrant smuggling, drug trafficking, and other transnational crimes," he said.
The prime minister thanked international partners for their support but stressed that generosity cannot become an excuse for political inaction.
“Nor can Bangladesh be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely. The crisis originated in Myanmar; its solution lies in Myanmar,” he said.
UN officials also pointed to the genocide case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), brought by The Gambia against Myanmar, stressing that justice must be an integral part of any lasting solution and that momentum towards accountability must not be lost.
“Victims deserve to see that we, as an international community, are doing our utmost to avoid a repeat of past horrors,” UNGA President Dr Rahman said.
UNHCR Salih said refugees deserve a future that goes beyond survival.
Drawing on his conversations with Rohingya refugees, he said many continue to hope for a return home, but that return must mean more than simply crossing a border, he said.
“It means returning with rights, being able to move freely, to go to school, to work, to access services, the ability to live alongside other communities without fear,” and have a pathway to citizenship.
“Our responsibility is to help make that future possible,” the UNHCR chief added.

item.title: Dhaka calls for collective action to make right to development a reality
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has said the realization of the right to development requires the commitment, responsibility and collective action of all nations.
She made the remarks while speaking at a high-level event on the right to development held at UN Headquarters in New York on Wednesday.
The event was convened by the President of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly and Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman during the high-level week.
It marked the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development, which recognises development as an inalienable human right and calls for inclusive, sustainable and participatory development.
The state minister highlighted the government’s pro-people development agenda including the Family Card and Farmer Card initiatives.
She also underscored the role of women and youth as partners in development and the vision of a “Rainbow Nation” where no one is left behind.
Shama Obaed proposed a few priorities that include a fairer global financial architecture, predictable and equitable development and climate finance, equitable access to technology and AI, and a legally binding framework to turn the right to development into accountability.
The event brought together Member States and stakeholders to reaffirm the right to development and advance shared prosperity, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Shama Obaed also represented Bangladesh at the annual ministerial meeting of the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) Focal Points Network held at the UN Headquarters in New York.
The meeting, convened by the Philippines, Italy and UN Women on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, marked 25 years of UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on WPS and focused on strengthening its implementation and accountability.
Recalling Bangladesh’s pioneering role in supporting Resolution 1325 as an elected Security Council member in 2000, the State Minister reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to women’s meaningful participation in decision-making.
She called for stronger women-led early warning and mediation, greater participation of women in peace processes, integration of WPS into climate and humanitarian action and stronger accountability for violations against women.
The state minister highlighted ongoing efforts to develop Bangladesh’s second WPS National Action Plan.
She also presented the Dhaka Dialogue, a Bangladesh-led initiative addressing digital harassment and AI-enabled abuse against women, and invited Member States to join its forthcoming Group of Friends.
The meeting brought together ministers and senior representatives from different countries to strengthen implementation of the UN WPS agenda and advance women’s leadership in peace and security.

item.title: Standard Chartered explores retail exit in Bangladesh
item.description:
Rumors are circulating in Bangladesh's banking sector that multinational lender Standard Chartered Bangladesh is preparing to exit its retail (consumer) banking operations in the country.
While the bank has not officially confirmed the move, industry sources report that negotiations have taken place with interested local buyers through a competitive process.
Regional and local senior executives have reportedly met with the Governor of Bangladesh Bank to discuss their plans.
Among local institutions, Brac Bank and City Bank are leading the race to acquire the portfolio.
Senior industry insiders clarify that Standard Chartered is not exiting Bangladesh entirely.
Instead, it is offloading its retail banking portfolio—which includes savings and current accounts, debit and credit cards, personal and home loans, ATMs, and mobile banking.
The multinational lender intends to retain its corporate and institutional banking division, servicing large corporate clients as usual.
Since Standard Chartered has not publicly disclosed the exact number of employees dedicated to its retail segment, the scale of potential job losses remains unclear.
In portfolio transfer deals, personnel transfer terms form a crucial component of the negotiation:
A deal does not guarantee automatic employment rollover to the acquiring institution, nor does it imply immediate termination for all staff.
Job retention will largely depend on the acquiring bank and the final terms of the agreement.
Key assets
Standard Chartered’s retail portfolio is a highly lucrative target for domestic lenders due to its affluent customer base and higher average deposit balances.
Standard Chartered Retail Financial Snapshot:
The portfolio encompasses premium reward cards, Islamic banking services, and specialized wealth management for Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs).

Officials from both Brac Bank and City Bank confirmed preliminary discussions, noting that any final acquisition remains subject to asset valuation, due diligence, and regulatory approval from Bangladesh Bank.
Broader strategic alignment
The potential sale aligns with Standard Chartered’s global strategy to optimize capital efficiency by scaling down retail banking in several emerging markets—including recent exits or downsizing across Africa, the Middle East, and Sri Lanka.
Compared to retail operations—which carry high overhead costs in compliance, technology, branches, and anti-money laundering (AML) controls—corporate banking and wealth management yield higher capital returns with fewer operational complexities.
This trend follows previous shifts among multinational banks in Bangladesh, including HSBC’s announcement to scale back retail operations in 2025 and American Express Bank's departure in 2005.
Bitopi Das Chowdhury, country head of corporate affairs, brand & marketing at Standard Chartered Bangladesh, dismissed the market discussions as speculative, stating: "We regularly review the efficiency of our global business model... Standard Chartered has a legacy of over 120 years in Bangladesh. We remain steadfast in our commitment to the country, and our operations continue as normal. Whatever is circulating in the market is just based on rumours and speculations."
Industry experts emphasize that if a sale proceeds, service continuity for existing retail clients is likely to remain smooth.
However, automatic account migration will depend on customer consent, account structures, and regulatory guidelines.

item.title: Speakers: Global cancer burden rising rapidly
item.description:
At the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong on Thursday, speakers warned that the global cancer burden is rising rapidly and that millions of patients still lack timely diagnosis and adequate care.
More than 2,000 delegates from 124 countries are attending the three-day congress, organized by the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) and the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society, to discuss prevention, early detection, treatment, and the need for more equitable cancer care worldwide.
The congress is taking place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Center from Thursday to Saturday.
Ulrika Årehed Kågström, president of the UICC, welcomed delegates and thanked the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society, local authorities, and representatives of China in Hong Kong for organizing the event.
She described the gathering as extraordinary, noting over 2,000 delegates from 124 countries and said, “Despite all these differences, we are united by a common purpose: to reduce cancer burden, address inequities, and improve survival.”
Ulrika stated that global cancer cases are projected to rise by 29% to 26.5 million annually by 2035, with deaths expected to increase by 37% to 12.9 million.
She noted that Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Oceania are experiencing a faster increase in cancer cases and deaths compared to North America and Europe.
She cautioned that access to quality cancer prevention, early detection, treatment, and supportive care remains highly unequal, with lower-income countries facing significant challenges in infrastructure, workforce capacity, treatment options, and affordability.
The estimated global economic cost of cancer from 2020 to 2050 was $25.2 trillion.
Ulrika stated that the UICC's new 10-year strategy prioritizes stronger cancer-control systems, increased investment in prevention and early detection, and more equitable access to treatment and care.
She also highlighted advances in targeted drugs, immunotherapy, CAR T-cell therapy, mRNA vaccines, and artificial intelligence, but cautioned that high costs and underdeveloped health systems prevent many patients from accessing these innovations.
“Progress by itself is not sufficient,” she said.
She stated that misinformation is hindering efforts to promote HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, even though these vaccines can prevent cancers.
She noted that although 81% of countries have national cancer-control plans, fewer than 10% are fully funded.
The president of the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society stated that cancer remains a leading cause of death in the city.
He emphasized the importance of public education, research, collaboration among medical professionals, and comprehensive support for patients and caregivers.
He explained that "prevent, fight and cure" is more than a motto; it is a mission to ensure every patient receives care and every caregiver is supported.
Eric Chan, Hong Kong's chief secretary, Professor Lo Chung-mau, the health secretary, and representatives from China's National Cancer Center, including Professor Jiemin Fang, attended the opening ceremony.
Fang said no country or organization could address the global cancer crisis alone.
He stated that solidarity, collaboration, and shared innovation are the most effective tools in the global fight against cancer.
He stated that the Congress will focus on people-centered cancer care, including prevention, screening, accurate diagnosis, innovative treatment, health policy reform, and rehabilitation.
The program included a pre-recorded message from Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization, who acknowledged progress in cancer control but noted that major inequalities persist.
He stated that global tobacco consumption has decreased by one-third and continues to decline in 140 countries, with cancer survival rates improving in many of them.
He said that scientific advances had made it possible "to dare to dream of eliminating cervical cancer worldwide".
Tedros noted that the World Health Organization's first global survey of people with cancer found that over half reported mental health issues, while the rest faced financial hardship, including selling their homes to pay for care.
Inequities continue to exist; there are still large differences in terms of survival between high- and low-income countries, and premature cancer death is increasing in 48 countries, Tedros said.
He focused on eliminating these gaps.
The congress will feature sessions on prevention, screening and early detection, cancer research and innovation, health systems and policies, cancer treatment and palliative care, tobacco control, and the experiences of people living with cancer.
Cancer specialists, researchers, policymakers, government representatives, patient organizations, civil-society groups, and private-sector representatives are attending this three-day conference.
A traditional Chinese lion dance show in vibrant colors was performed on the main stage during the opening ceremony.

item.title: Biman signs deal to buy 11 more Boeing aircraft
item.description:
Biman Bangladesh Airlines has signed an agreement with US aircraft manufacturer Boeing to buy 11 more aircraft as Bangladesh moves to expand its aviation sector and open new routes, Prime Minister’s Adviser Mahdi Amin said on Wednesday.
“A significant signing ceremony was held with Boeing today [Wednesday], where Biman Bangladesh Airlines signed an agreement to purchase 11 more Boeing aircraft,” he said at a press briefing at the Hyatt Grand Central New York.
Mahdi said Biman Chairman Rumee A Hossain signed the agreement on behalf of the national flag carrier.
He said Bangladesh is buying aircraft based on its own requirements as the aviation sector is expanding. “We buy aircraft based on our needs. We want to expand our aviation sector, and for that we need aircraft,” he said.
The adviser said Bangladesh has a long-standing commercial relationship with Boeing, while discussions with Airbus could also take place based on the country’s requirements.
“The two companies that provide good aircraft are Boeing and Airbus. We will buy from Boeing or Airbus according to our needs. No one will force us to buy either,” he said.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said the signing ceremony was significant as several senior US government officials attended the event.
US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Under Secretary of Commerce William Kimmitt, Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Paul Kapur and Special Representative for Commercial and Business Affairs Vinay Chawla attended the ceremony.
Kobir said the presence of the senior US officials demonstrated the importance of Bangladesh-US relations.
He said the participation of senior officials from the US Commerce and State Departments showed that the two countries are looking at expanding trade and investment while strengthening bilateral relations.
Referring to President Donald Trump’s recent letter to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the state minister said the US President had expressed his appreciation for Bangladesh’s decision to purchase Boeing aircraft and conveyed confidence in the country’s future under Tarique Rahman’s leadership.
He said the Boeing agreement was also important from the perspective of expanding Bangladesh’s aviation sector and strengthening economic ties with the United States.
Mahdi said the Boeing delegation later held a courtesy meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
In April, Bangladesh signed a deal with Boeing to purchase 14 aircraft for Biman in a deal valued at $3.7 billion, described as the airline’s biggest-ever aircraft order.
In a letter to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on September 1, Trump thanked him for the decision to purchase Boeing aircraft and said Boeing would not let Bangladesh down.
Mahdi said technical assessments and discussions were also underway on possible future aircraft purchases, including from Airbus, based on Bangladesh’s requirements.
He said Bangladesh is expanding its aviation sector, planning new routes and will need additional aircraft to meet growing demand.
Kobir said Bangladesh will continue to assess its requirements before making further aircraft purchases, adding that the government wants to ensure that its aviation expansion serves the country’s interests.
The Boeing signing was among a series of activities during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s four-day visit to New York to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
The signing ceremony was attended by Brad McMullen, Boeing senior vice president of Commercial Sales and Marketing, and Rumee A Hossain, chairman of Biman Bangladesh Airlines, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat, Kobir, Mahdi, Invest Bangladesh Authority Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, Howard Lutnick and Christopher Landau on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

item.title: UNGA81: PM calls for urgent global action on climate crisis, predictable finance
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday called for five urgent global actions to tackle climate change and ensure a just and equitable transition, including meeting the 1.5°C target and ensuring predictable climate finance.
“Collective action based on “Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities” is imperative…We call for 5 urgent actions,” he said.
Tarique made the call while addressing a high-level meeting on “Climate Action and the Just Transition” at the UN Headquarters in New York.
Outlining the five urgent actions, the Prime Minister first called for achieving the 1.5°C global warming limit through global emission cuts, as set out in the Paris Agreement.
Second, Tarique called for predictable and accessible finance for adaptation in climate-vulnerable countries.
Third, he urged greater access to climate-smart technologies to enable a just and equitable climate transition.
Fourth, Tarique stressed the need for expanding renewable energy through accessible finance, capacity-building and technology transfer.
And fifth, he called for full implementation and regular replenishment of the Loss and Damage Fund.
“Bangladesh seeks partnerships that help us implement our plans. Let us act together to build a safer and more sustainable future for generations to come,” the Prime Minister added.
Tarique said Bangladesh contributes less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions but is among the most climate-vulnerable countries.
He said Bangladesh could lose 12 to 18% of its coastal areas to sea-level rise by the end of this century, affecting the livelihoods of tens of millions of people.
“Climate change has caused loss and damage equivalent to 1% of our GDP. Our food security is at serious risk,” Tarique said.
The prime minister said Bangladesh had allocated nearly $3.19 billion in its budget for climate adaptation but warned that the country risked severe damage without international support.
He said Bangladesh plans to plant 250 million trees over five years and dig around 20,000 kilometres of rivers and canals, alongside the Padma Barrage and Teesta Barrage Master Plan, to retain water, reduce flood risks, revive wetlands and recharge groundwater.
The government also aims to generate 20% of the country's electricity demand from renewable sources by 2030, Tarique said.
Bangladesh is promoting green industries, including jute products, eco-friendly transport, waste-to-energy and circular economy initiatives, while developing a national carbon market, he said adding that, “But we cannot succeed in isolation.”
The high-level meeting was held at the Trusteeship Council Chamber of the UN Headquarters as part of the Prime Minister's engagements during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

item.title: Getting support for the Rohingya
item.description:
It is encouraging to see Bangladesh taking active measures to put renewed pressure on the international community to help resolve the Rohingya crisis, and facilitate their safe, voluntary, and dignified return to Myanmar.
During his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman sought continued international cooperation for a sustainable solution to the crisis during a meeting with UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy on Myanmar Julie Bishop. Bangladesh also co-hosted a high-level side event on the Rohingya crisis, aimed at renewing international political and humanitarian support and strengthening accountability efforts.
These are undoubtedly important steps. For years, Bangladesh has carried an enormous humanitarian responsibility while the Rohingya have remained trapped in prolonged displacement. Now, more than nine years after the massive influx of 2017, the crisis cannot be allowed to become an accepted permanent reality.
International concern has produced humanitarian assistance, statements, and diplomatic engagement, but these have yet to deliver the outcome Bangladesh and the Rohingya need most: A safe and sustainable return home.
As Bangladesh has rightly emphasized, repatriation cannot simply mean crossing the border. Myanmar must provide conditions that guarantee security, rights, and dignity.
That is why sustained international pressure is essential. The UN, regional powers, and other influential countries must do more to address the conditions that have prevented meaningful repatriation. Myanmar must also face continued pressure to create an environment in which the Rohingya can return voluntarily and with confidence in their future.
Bangladesh should continue using every diplomatic platform available to keep this issue at the forefront of international attention. The current efforts are a welcome indication that we are not prepared to let the crisis fade from the global agenda.
We have wanted successful repatriation for years; it is time to finally make it happen. Continued diplomacy must now translate into coordinated international action, concrete pressure and, ultimately, a dignified return for the Rohingya to their homeland.

item.title: Ending our culture of impunity
item.description:
The deaths of two people in separate road incidents in Dhaka this week have exposed a long-standing problem that goes beyond reckless driving or unfortunate accidents: The persistence of a culture in which accountability too often comes after tragedy, if at all.
24-year-old construction worker Mehedi Hasan Mir was killed by a car that ran over him on a footpath, with a 16-year-old detained for the incident. In a separate case, 50-year-old Meherun Begum with hearing disabilities was killed by a DNCC garbage truck while collecting recyclable materials.
These cases underline just how vulnerable ordinary citizens remain in spaces that should be safe. They also raise questions about who is responsible when vehicles are operated without adequate safeguards, when drivers fail to exercise due care, or when public authorities do not sufficiently protect people working or living around their operations.
We have seen too many incidents followed by familiar promises of investigation and action, only for public attention to move on. That cannot be allowed to become the end of the process.
Every death on the road must lead to a credible investigation, clear determination of responsibility and, where warranted, meaningful legal consequences.
Accountability must apply equally, regardless of wealth, family connections, or institutional position. The same principle must govern public bodies such as city corporations; government vehicles and private cars alike must be subject to the law.
Ending impunity also requires prevention through stricter enforcement, safer vehicle operations, proper driver training, better monitoring, and protection for pedestrians and vulnerable workers.
A city cannot call itself safe when people can lose their lives simply by resting on a footpath or collecting recyclable materials.
Justice must be ensured for these deaths -- and the countless other similar tragedies that have plagued our streets for too long.
More importantly, however, the system must be made into one that ensures that fewer families are left seeking this kind of justice in the first place.

item.title: Bangladesh’s next leap?
item.description:
Over the years, I have sat on many sides of the same economic story.
I have seen it through the eyes of a microfinance borrower, a migrant, a family separated by borders and, today, a technology entrepreneur building in Silicon Valley.
Those experiences have convinced me of something: Bangladesh’s next great financial transformation will not come from one technology. It will come from connecting technology to the realities of ordinary people.
My first exposure to that reality came through Grameen Bank.
Working in microfinance taught me that financial inclusion is not simply about giving someone access to money. It is about giving people the ability to make decisions, take control of their economic lives, and create opportunities that previously seemed out of reach.
I learned an important lesson there: Capital is powerful, but knowledge and access determine how effectively people can use it.
Years later, at the UN migration agency, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), I encountered another side of the equation.
I worked directly with migrants and saw the human story behind migration statistics. People weren’t simply “sending remittances.” They were working thousands of miles from home to pay for a child’s education, build a house, support parents or create a better future for their families.
A remittance is therefore not just a financial transaction. It is a sacrifice converted into hope.
Then, working in the visa section of the Swedish Embassy, I spent years speaking with migrants and families navigating the complexities of moving across borders.
That experience taught me something else: Behind every application, transaction, and statistic is a human being trying to move forward.
Today, from Silicon Valley, I see a fourth piece of the puzzle.
I see what happens when software, artificial intelligence, and modern financial infrastructure are designed to remove friction from everyday life.
And it raises a question I cannot ignore: What if Bangladesh could combine the lessons of microfinance, the realities of migration, and the power of AI to fundamentally change what happens to every taka that comes home?
That is the opportunity in front of us.
From remittances to wealth
Bangladesh has become a global remittance powerhouse.
Millions of Bangladeshis work abroad and send money home, with remittances reaching approximately $35.6 billion in FY2025-26.
But sending money internationally remains surprisingly expensive and complicated.
A worker in Riyadh, New York, or London may initiate a transfer that passes through several financial intermediaries before his family receives taka in Rangpur, Sylhet, or Barisal.
The technology of the internet has made information instantaneous. Yet moving money can still feel like sending a letter by courier.
We should ask a more ambitious question: What if the world’s financial infrastructure moved at internet speed?
This is where Web 3.0 and regulated digital-dollar settlement become interesting. Stablecoins such as USDC or USDT are digital currencies designed to maintain a stable value, typically by being backed by reserves such as US dollars or highly liquid assets. In simple terms, they are a way of representing dollar value digitally and moving it over the internet.
Their more important long-term potential may be as financial infrastructure, rather than as speculative instruments.
The United States has now formally recognized this potential. The GENIUS Act, signed into law in 2025, established a federal regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, including requirements around reserves, redemption, and oversight.
Traditional financial institutions are also building in this direction.
JP Morgan, for example, has launched JPM Coin as a bank-issued digital deposit token that allows institutional clients to move and settle US dollars on blockchain networks around the clock. Other major financial institutions, including Bank of America, Citi, and Goldman Sachs, are also exploring dollar-denominated digital settlement infrastructure.
The distinction is important: Bank-issued deposit tokens are not necessarily the same thing as stablecoins such as USDC.
But they demonstrate something significant: The world’s largest financial institutions increasingly see blockchain-based digital money and programmable settlement as an evolution of financial infrastructure.
For ordinary people, the concept can be much simpler: A dollar with an internet connection. The customer doesn’t need to understand blockchain. They shouldn’t have to.
What matters is whether regulated technology can make money move faster, more transparently, and at lower cost, while maintaining the protections people expect from the financial system.
Dollar in. Taka out. A regulated institution initiates the transaction abroad.
Digital settlement infrastructure moves the value. A licensed Bangladesh-side institution receives it, converts it into taka, and delivers it to the recipient’s bank or approved mobile financial account.
The technology does the complicated work behind the scenes. The customer gets a faster, simpler experience.
And this is not merely theoretical. An IMF study estimated roughly $2 trillion in stablecoin transactions during 2024, with approximately $633bn in North America and $519bn in Asia and the Pacific.
Relative to economic size, activity was particularly significant in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Africa and the Middle East.
For Bangladesh, however, this must not become an excuse to abandon prudent regulation. The question is not whether Bangladesh should blindly embrace Web 3.0. It is whether Bangladesh can responsibly experiment with regulated digital settlement for remittances.
One corridor. Licensed institutions. Full KYC and AML controls.
Strict transaction limits. Transparent reporting. Mandatory conversion into taka with Bangladesh Bank firmly in control.
The objective is not less regulation. It is better infrastructure underneath effective regulation.
Faster money is only half the revolution
My experience at Grameen Bank keeps bringing me back to the same realization: Access without understanding is incomplete inclusion.
Imagine a migrant worker asking an AI assistant in Bangla: “আমি প্রতি মাসে ৫,০০০ টাকা সঞ্চয় করলে পাঁচ বছর পরে কত হবে?”
Imagine a mother receiving a remittance asking: “How much should I save for my children’s education?”
Imagine a first-time investor asking: “What is a bond? What is a stock? What is inflation?”
Today, we can build AI systems that answer these questions instantly, patiently, and in the user’s own language.
This is more than a chatbot. It could become a personal financial tutor for an entire country. It could teach budgeting, savings, investing, insurance, debt management, and fraud prevention.
With agentic AI, people can eventually do more than ask questions. AI agents can help execute financial tasks and, under carefully defined controls, potentially transactions.
But this is precisely where we must be careful. The same AI that can democratize financial knowledge can democratize financial fraud.
AI can generate convincing scams, impersonate voices, create fake documents, manipulate users, and produce confident but unsuitable financial advice.
So AI-powered financial inclusion must be built with safety by design, not safety as an afterthought.
That means strong data-privacy protections, clear disclosure when people are interacting with AI, continuous fraud monitoring, suitability and risk checks before financial recommendations, audit trails for AI-driven actions, and human oversight for high-impact decisions.
AI should explain before it acts. And when the stakes are high, a human should remain in the loop.
The goal is not to replace financial professionals or regulators. It is to give them better tools -- and give ordinary people better access to knowledge.
The smartphone could become more than a wallet. It could become Bangladesh’s most accessible financial classroom.
Imagine connecting the two
This is where the vision becomes bigger than payments.
Imagine a Bangladeshi worker in New York sends $500 home. The transaction moves through a regulated Web 3.0 settlement rail. A licensed institution in Bangladesh converts the funds into taka. The family receives the money.
Then the AI financial assistant asks: “Would you like to see what you could save over the next year?”
It helps them build a budget. It explains compound interest. It identifies potential financial risks. It teaches them how to avoid scams. And, where appropriate, it explains regulated savings and investment products.
The journey changes from:
Remittance → Spending
to:
Remittance → Financial Literacy → Saving → Investing → Wealth Creation.
That is the transformation I believe Bangladesh should pursue.
The diaspora is our global economic network
My years working with migrants changed how I think about the Bangladeshi diaspora.
We often talk about migrants as a source of foreign currency. But that is only one dimension of their value.
They are workers, entrepreneurs, investors, professionals, consumers, and bridges between Bangladesh and the global economy.
They don’t just send money. They send knowledge, aspirations, relationships, and eventually, capital.
What if Bangladesh built financial infrastructure designed around that reality? What if a Bangladeshi in New York could send money home and, through the same trusted ecosystem, understand how to invest in a Bangladeshi business?
What if someone in London could support their family while also building a long-term investment portfolio connected to Bangladesh?
What if remittances became the gateway through which the diaspora participated more deeply in the country’s economic future?
Then the objective changes. We are no longer simply trying to increase remittances. We are trying to increase the economic value created by every remitted dollar.
Build the future. Don’t wait for it
We don’t need to transform the entire financial system tomorrow. We can start with a controlled experiment.
Take the United States-Bangladesh corridor.
Bring together Bangladesh Bank, licensed banks, remittance providers, regulated digital-dollar infrastructure companies, and technology platforms.
Create a sandbox. Set strict limits. Monitor every transaction. Measure settlement times, costs, FX spreads, formal-channel usage, AML outcomes, and customer experience.
For AI, measure something equally important: Accuracy, fraud detection, consumer complaints, inappropriate recommendations, data protection, and human-override rates.
Then let evidence -- not ideology -- determine what happens next.
If it works, scale it. If it doesn’t, learn from it.
The most innovative countries in the world aren’t necessarily those that remove every rule. They are the countries that learn how to innovate safely.
From microfinance to AI
When I look at my own journey -- from Grameen Bank, to working with migrants at IOM, to sitting across from families at the Swedish Embassy, and now building technology in Silicon Valley -- I see a common thread.
The technology has changed dramatically. The human aspirations have not.
People still want the same things.
A better life. A safer future. An education for their children. A home. Financial security. An opportunity to build something of their own.
What has changed is our ability to build systems capable of helping millions pursue those goals simultaneously.
Microfinance showed the world that financial inclusion could start at the grassroots.
Mobile financial services showed Bangladesh that technology could put financial tools into the hands of millions.
AI now gives us the possibility of putting personalized financial intelligence into the hands of everyone.
And modern digital settlement gives us the possibility of moving money across borders with dramatically less friction.
Put those pieces together, and something much bigger emerges.
Bangladesh does not need to become the world’s Web 3.0 capital. It needs to become a country where:
That is the vision. A future where the Bangladeshi worker abroad doesn’t simply send money home. He sends the opportunity home.
Where the family receiving that money doesn’t simply spend it. They learn, save, and invest.
Where the smartphone doesn’t simply transfer money. It teaches a child about compound interest.
Where financial infrastructure doesn’t simply process transactions. It helps build trust.
And where Bangladesh doesn’t simply consume the next generation of financial technology. It helps build it.
My experiences in Bangladesh, with migrants and with families, taught me something more important: The best technology is not the technology that looks most futuristic. It is the technology that makes ordinary people’s lives better.
Bangladesh has the talent, the diaspora, the scale, and the entrepreneurial energy to lead this next chapter. We don’t need to wait for the future of finance to arrive.
We can build a Bangladesh that is ready for it -- and help shape what that future looks like.
And after generations of Bangladeshis sending money home, perhaps it is finally time for the money to arrive before the tea gets cold.
Farihan F Rahman is a Bangladeshi technology entrepreneur and founder of InveStar, a Silicon Valley AI wealth-tech company. He is a Director of Startup Grind, the world’s largest startup community, a Draper Champion, and Perplexity AI fellow.

item.title: In the global staging of a refugee crisis, language is sovereign
item.description:
Language is slippery, often subversive. When Burma became Myanmar in 1989, this was the ruling junta’s most overt disavowal of the colonial past. In striking out Britain’s name for the nation, the military attempted to put forth a new image.
The old name, derived from the dominant Bamar ethnic group, was replaced in a sort of semantic trick. It suggested the nation, this new Myanmar, welcomed all ethnic groups composing the vast country.
Junta control would go on to ebb and surge amid the stuttering thrust of “true democracy” -- as it does, as it will -- but that new name, the national veneer, the nom de plume to dissemble the nom de guerre , was largely accepted. Most of the world today indeed recognizes the name “Myanmar.”
Manipulations of language have proven effective tools for the authority of Myanmar. The explosive consequences of these actions are laid bare in decades of ethnic cleansing and genocide of the minority Rohingya, over a million of whom now seek refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh.
While linguistic exploitations by Myanmar state perpetrators have been scrutinized, however, a parallel adaptation of language concerning the refugees by humanitarian systems and host nations has been largely overlooked, despite this language increasingly compromising the welfare of the Rohingya.
Re-evaluating the standard lexicon of the aid system now is critical. Bangladesh presides for the first time over the 81st session of the UN General Assembly which opened in September and has high-level conferences and general debate scheduled this week.
At the helm of the UNGA is foreign minister Khalilur Rahman, selected in a historic election this past June, who was previously the High Representative on Rohingya Issues during the interim government of Bangladesh.
This is an unprecedented position with high potentiality, given Khalilur Rahman’s expertise (coupled with Bangladesh’s election of new Prime Minister Tarique Rahman) but will the old rhetoric staging the refugees’ condition -- ineffective, often counterproductive -- be finally retired?
Sweeping language abounded in the listed objectives for the UN’s first high-level conference on the Rohingya and other minorities of Myanmar which took place in September 2025. The UN organ published aims of the conference ahead of last year’s meeting, including to “review the overall [Rohingya] crisis and address its root causes,” the aspirational outcome of which being “a comprehensive, innovative and concrete plan for a sustainable resolution of the crisis.”
The head of Bangladesh’s interim government at that time, Muhammad Yunus, put forth an address at that meeting which included a seven point plan concerning the Rohingya in Bangladesh. The entirety of this address, however, did not include the word “refugee” to describe those displaced under conditions of war and genocide.
And though this was yet another appeal by the Bangladesh administration to the global community for aid concerning the Rohingya, the displaced population in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh (composing the largest camp system in the world) are still not recognized de jure by the Bangladesh government via the term “refugees.”
Instead, they are designated “Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals” (FDMN). Bangladesh also continues to abstain from ratifying the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol, a decision that allows the nation to circumvent certain mechanisms of international refugee protection frameworks and law.
Systemic manufactures disguised as intrinsic flaw
Yunus also stated during that September 2025 UN meeting: “Bangladesh is a victim of the crisis. We are forced to bear huge financial, social, and environmental costs. Criminal activities…threaten our social fabric.”
The portrayal of Bangladesh as a “victim” of a crisis, closely juxtaposed with the formulaic generalization of the Rohingya as “criminal,” is also a calculated linguistic -- ideological -- construction.
Notably, the Rohingya are largely financially supported by international donor groups and other foreign governments (covering over 90% of the Rohingya Joint Response Plan in 2025), and Bangladesh has in fact experienced local economic development in Cox’s Bazar from the influx of foreign aid and personnel.
Moreover, Bangladesh bars the Rohingya from legal higher education or employment opportunities, so the refugees are often forced into markets which exploit Rohingya workers for further economic gain.
The language of criminality as it pertains to the Rohingya, then, presents a sustained and systemic manufacture as an intrinsic attribute. Bangladesh has in fact extracted a certain legitimacy and foothold through perpetuated Rohingya containment.
Furthermore, the language of a helpless saviour, a victim of an unsavory population, as reinforced by Bangladesh’s highest office, has been co-opted by other host nations to devastating effect.
Harms of international aid community language
The characterization of the refugees in the greater international aid community must also be assessed. The words “burden” and “burden-sharing” (a term which has its genesis at the inception of the UNHCR) are near-universal phraseology for deliverables related to refugee solutions development.
Though this language has been modified at times through the expanded term “burden and responsibility sharing” (this term appearing in documents concerning the high-level UN conference on the Rohingya), the diction invariably confounds sustainable solutions development.
Expediency, asymmetrical compromise, and generalization become the dominant undercurrents of conversation, often influencing safety and longevity considerations. The refugee community of Cox’s Bazar thus become the load to cast off, an onus of little apparent value (humanistic, capitalistic, all that lies between).
Host nations certainly require assistance of international bodies to manage massive refugee populations. These bodies must be cognizant of the unintended effects of modern aid solicitation language.
A major component of this aid solicitation language is made manifest by the international community’s recurring description (see Yunus’ aforementioned speech) of the Rohingya refugees’ condition as a “crisis.”
The hackneyed term is somewhat a misnomer when describing the state of refugees. The connotations of “crisis” elicit ideas of acute, natural phenomena: Successions of events by which victims and witnesses alike are vulnerable, with this state of “crisis” materializing no obvious perpetrators.
In recent headlines relating to the Rohingya, ample mention is made of a humanitarian disaster, a population that is aid-dependent. Less emphasis and fewer details concerning the Myanmar authority are expounded upon, leaving the refugees an abstraction isolated from the political and historical events which made them refugees.
Retiring a philosophy of rhetoric
The first high-level conference on the Rohingya at the UN concluded last year with further aid commitments from a few nations, though funding remains significantly short of targets. The issues facing Rohingya in Bangladesh also persist, with no real success in developing repatriation pathways or resettlement policies for the refugees.
Notably, however, there is fertile ground for reform at the moment. Bangladesh has transitioned from its interim government to a new administration on the wings of renewed democratic process and promise for inclusive national change. Moreover, with Khalilur Rahman at the helm of the UNGA, he will oversee numerous agendas, including the old call for a “sustainable resolution” for the ongoing displacement and genocide of the Rohingya.
There will be speeches insisting that promises and pledges translate this time to “real action,” and by this these parties will gesture to policy change. Inaction stems, though, not only from empty words. The recycling of an old lexicon, an entire philosophy of influential rhetoric, must be retired.
Farihah Ahmed received her MFA in Writing from Columbia University. She is the founder and director of RoVena, a global civil society organization which advocates for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh.

Ajmul murder: Asif claims video recorded of forced confession
item.description:
A newly arrested suspect in the Ajmul murder case has told the Special Response Battalion (SRB) that the victim was tortured and forced to confess to stealing rice, a mobile phone and money, with a video recorded during the interrogation.
Sheikh Asif Hossain, a former Khulna University student, also told SRB-6 that Ajmul fell to the ground after slipping while attempting to jump from the fourth-floor roof to the third floor to escape those assaulting him, according to the battalion.
SRB-6 Commander Lt Col Nistar Ahmed said Asif was arrested in Bhatiyapara, Gopalganj. He is the son of Sheikh Miraj of Sanatankati village in Paikgacha upazila, Khulna.
After preliminary interrogation, Asif was handed over to Harintana police station under Khulna Metropolitan Police for further legal action.
According to the SRB commander, Asif had secured a job at a private bank and was scheduled to join on September 20, but went into hiding after Ajmul’s death on the night of September 18.
During interrogation, Asif said he had gone to the building on Friday night to meet classmates from his university batch. He was present when Ajmul was allegedly beaten inside a room.
He said Ajmul was later taken to the fourth-floor roof and assaulted. Those present allegedly tried to force him to confess to stealing rice, a mobile phone and money, while several people recorded videos of his statements.
According to Asif’s account, Ajmul was subsequently threatened with being handed over to police. Fearing arrest, Ajmul attempted to jump from the fourth floor to the third floor but slipped and fell to the ground, sustaining serious injuries. He later died after being taken to hospital.
Asif also told the SRB that mess manager Mehedi and Habib Hasnat Rifat, a cash officer at Krishi Bank’s Town Noapara branch, were directly involved in the incident. He alleged that Rifat played a significant role in beating Ajmul, but said there was no intention to kill him.
He also identified Tarek, alias Rubel, owner of Ma-Babar Doa Tanha Juice Corner in front of Khaja Hall, as another person who physically assaulted Ajmul.
Harintana police station Officer-in-Charge Md Iqbal Hossain said four people have been arrested in connection with the case since the night of September 18.
The arrested suspects include three former Khulna University students and a juice shop owner, he said.
Iqbal said Rifat gave a confessional statement before a court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on September 22, followed by Pratap and Rubel on September 23.
He said the suspects provided information during police interrogation, which is being reviewed and verified. Asif is scheduled to be produced before a court on September 24 and may also give a voluntary statement.
The OC said further information could emerge if mess manager Mehedi is arrested.
Ajmul, a first-year English student at North Western University, was allegedly beaten at a four-storey building on Islamnagar Road, near Khulna University’s Hall Road, on the night of September 18 over allegations of stealing rice.
He subsequently fell from the building and died. His relatives have alleged that he was beaten to death.
On September 19, Ajmul’s father, Kutubuddin, filed a murder case with Harintana police station, naming four Khulna University students and accusing 20-25 unidentified people.
Four people have so far been arrested in connection with the case.

item.title: Dhaka records ‘moderate’ air quality Thursday morning
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 37th among the world's most polluted cities on Thursday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 64 at 10:22am.
The air quality was classified as "moderate", indicating that the air quality is generally acceptable, although unusually sensitive people may experience some health effects, according to the AQI scale.
DR Congo’s Kinshasa topped the list with an AQI score of 239.
Malaysia’s Kuching and Pakistan’s Lahore jointly ranked second, with AQI scores of 194 each.
Dubai, United Arab Emirates, ranked third, with an AQI score of 157.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

Hockey team beat Sri Lanka 5-1 for first Asian Games win
item.description:
Bangladesh clinched their first victory in the 20th Asian Games men’s hockey competition, beating Sri Lanka 5-1 in their Pool A encounter at Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium in Nagoya, Japan on Thursday.
Amirul Islam and Ashraful Islam scored two goals each, while Mahbub Hossain added the other for the red and green brigade.
Bangladesh dominated from the outset and took the lead in the eighth minute when Amirul converted a penalty corner.
They doubled their advantage in the 16th minute through another penalty corner, with Ashraful finding the target.
Sri Lanka’s Weerappuli Kusal pulled one back two minutes later by converting a penalty corner, but Bangladesh continued to control proceedings.
Amirul restored Bangladesh’s two-goal cushion in the 27th minute before Mahbub added another in the 43rd minute, both from penalty corners.
Ashraful completed the scoring in the 54th minute by converting a penalty stroke to seal a comfortable victory for Bangladesh.
Bangladesh earned 18 penalty corners throughout the match, keeping the Sri Lankan defence under sustained pressure.
The victory marked Bangladesh’s first win in the men’s hockey competition at the ongoing Asian Games.
Bangladesh began their campaign with a 5-0 defeat to South Korea before suffering a 6-1 loss to hosts Japan in their second group match.
The men in red and green will play their remaining Pool A matches against Indonesia and India on September 26 and 28 respectively at the same venue.

item.title: India to host first cycling world championships
item.description:
Cycling's Road World Championships will head to India for the first time as the 2032 edition was awarded to the world's most populous nation on Wednesday.
Pune -- a city of around seven million people, some 100 miles (160 kilometers) from Mumbai -- beat competition from the Dutch city of Groningen in a vote at the International Cycling Union (UCI) congress in Montreal.
Groningen will receive the 2034 edition, said organizers, following the vote held during this year's ongoing championships.
"There were two very good, solid bids and I think we have found a good solution for both organizers," said UCI president David Lappartient.
India is already preparing to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games, in Ahmedabad, and has ambitions to host the 2036 Olympics.
After decades exclusively in Europe, the first Cycling World Championships in North America took place in Montreal in 1974.
Japan was the first Asian country to host the event, in 1990, followed by Doha in 2016 and Abu Dhabi, which will host the 2028 edition.
Last year, Rwanda became the first African country to host the event.

item.title: Ronaldo says he can still help Portugal despite criticism
item.description:
Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered ending his international career after the World Cup, while acknowledging that some critics in Portugal want him to leave the national team.
The 41-year-old forward was confirmed by coach Jorge Jesus as a starter for his 234th appearance for Portugal, against Wales on Thursday in the Nations League.
Asked at a pre-match news conference whether he had considered retiring from international football after Portugal's round-of-16 defeat to Spain in July, Ronaldo said he had.
“Yes, I did. Of course, I'm always thinking about my decisions, my future, the present also,” he said.
Ronaldo said he had discussed his future with Portugal's president and Jesus, who previously coached Ronaldo at Saudi club Al-Nassr and led the team to the Saudi league title in May.
“I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want, and I will finish when I feel like I'm not doing anything here,” he said.
Ronaldo, who led Portugal to the Nations League title in 2025, is also closing in on 1,000 career goals.
“This is a new young generation,” he said. “But for me, the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score goals and help the team win games.”
Ronaldo also acknowledged that he remains a target of criticism in his home country.
“I feel the Portuguese fans like me, but I do understand that some TV channels want to criticize me,” he said.
“They are dying for me not to come to the national team any more, but I can still move away from it.”
Ronaldo said he has become accustomed to criticism after more than two decades in the spotlight.
“I'm used to it. For over 20 years I have been doing this, but my memories are with people who love me,” he said.
He added that he hopes to remain an example for younger generations even after retiring.
“I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired… in 10 years,” Ronaldo said with a smile.

item.description:

Speaking at a meeting on law and order and development in Bogra, he said officials may have personal political choices but remain accountable to the people for delivering services and implementing development programmes.
Bari said government postings and promotions are being made on the basis of transparency, honesty and competence. He also outlined plans to develop Bogura as an economic hub through an airport, agro-based industries, an international-standard university and increased investment in small and medium enterprises.
He highlighted new social safety programmes, including family, farmer and health cards, as well as initiatives on education, nutrition, environmental protection and safe drinking water.

item.title: Education Minister: Govt plans specialised university on blue economy
item.description:
The government is working on the blue economy and plans to establish a specialised university focusing on the sector in the future, Education Minister Dr A N M Ehsanul Hoque Milon said on Wednesday.
He made the remarks while addressing a scholarship distribution ceremony organised jointly by the Marketing Alumni Association of Dhaka University and Meghna Group of Industries (MGI) at the Nabab Nawab Ali Chowdhury Senate Building.
The minister said the government is working to develop Bangladesh’s human resources by equipping them with the skills needed for the future.
“The government is working with the highest priority on the education sector to improve the country’s education system,” he said.
Highlighting the importance of exposure to diverse cultures and experiences, Milon said such exposure enables people to analyse problems from multiple perspectives.
He urged students not to confine themselves to a single field but to apply their knowledge, talents and skills across different areas.
Speaking about the gap between academia and industry, the education minister said major companies and industries in Bangladesh do not give sufficient importance to strengthening linkages between the two sectors.
“It is unfortunate that big companies and industries in our country do not attach enough importance to academia-industry linkage,” he said.
Referring to China, he said industries there have established polytechnic institutes within industrial facilities, allowing engineers to teach students while students gain practical experience by working in those industries. “Such a linkage is also necessary in our country,” he added.
“The people before me today will build the Bangladesh of tomorrow. Our intellect is in no way inferior to that of citizens of other countries,” he said addressing the students.
Milon praised MGI’s corporate social responsibility initiative of providing scholarships to university students and urged other corporate organizations to come forward with similar initiatives to support education.
The event, titled ‘MGI-MAA Scholarship 2026,’ was organised jointly by MGI and the DU Marketing Department Alumni Association to provide scholarships to 90 students of the Marketing Department of DU.

item.title: Six decades on, Dinajpur BSCIC still struggles with basic services
item.description:
Despite more than six decades of operation and Tk 225.50 crore in investment, the BSCIC Industrial Estate in Dinajpur is still struggling to provide basic infrastructure and services to its entrepreneurs.
Established in 1962, the industrial estate has generated employment for nearly 4,825 people. Yet it continues to face longstanding problems, including the absence of a boundary wall, inadequate drainage, poor waste management and waterlogging during the rainy season.
Entrepreneurs say the lack of essential facilities is disrupting industrial operations and discouraging new investment in the estate.
The Bangladesh Small and Cottage Industries Corporation (BSCIC) established the industrial estate on 35.14 acres of land in the Pulhat area of Dinajpur town in 1962 at a cost of Tk 45.54 lakh. The project was completed in 1972.
Initially, 189 industrial plots were allocated, covering 28.74 acres. According to BSCIC data, 54 industrial units are currently located in the estate, of which 52 are operational. Two units—M/s Habiba Aluminium Industries (Pvt.) Ltd and M/s Rupon Oil and Feeds (Pvt.) Ltd—are closed due to bank loan defaults, with related cases pending in court.
The estate houses a diverse range of industries, including food processing, rice milling, engineering, chemical, timber, bakery, silver, automated flour milling, pulse and edible oil processing.
There are 33 A-type plots measuring 15,000 square feet each, 42 B-type plots of 9,000 square feet, 64 C-type plots of 4,500 square feet and 65 D-type plots of 2,250 square feet.
BSCIC data show that the industrial units have created employment for around 4,825 workers and employees, including 3,377 men and 1,448 women. Total investment stands at Tk 225.50 crore, while the annual value of production is Tk 302.58 crore.
The industrial estate generates Tk 201.54 lakh in annual government revenue from various sources. This includes Tk 165 lakh in income tax and VAT, Tk 1.35 lakh from electricity, Tk 4.26 lakh in land development tax, Tk 0.90 lakh in municipal tax, Tk 30 lakh in service charges and transfer fees, and Tk 0.03 lakh from telephone services.
The absence of a boundary wall has raised security concerns, while the inadequate drainage system causes waterlogging during the rainy season. The stagnant water makes movement difficult for workers and hampers the transportation of raw materials and finished goods.
Entrepreneurs have also complained about the accumulation of garbage in and around the industrial area, saying inadequate infrastructure and services are increasing their operating costs.
They said they pay an annual service charge of Tk 3.50 per square foot. Including VAT and land-related charges, the total comes to Tk 4.31 per square foot. Despite paying the charges regularly, they alleged that the services provided by the authorities do not meet their needs.
Md Nuruzzaman Sarker, president of the Dinajpur Rice Mill Owners' Group, called for immediate measures to improve the drainage system, construct a boundary wall and strengthen security at the estate.
Md Abu Bakar Siddiq, president of the Dinajpur Chamber of Commerce and Industry and owner of an auto-rice mill, said service charges are increasing every year, while the quality of services remains inadequate.
“New entrepreneurs are losing interest as a result. New investment cannot be encouraged without proper services and government support,” he said.
BSCIC officials, however, said they have taken initiatives to address the problems.
Md Jahedul Islam, deputy general manager of Dinajpur BSCIC, acknowledged the shortcomings, including the lack of a boundary wall and problems with roads, drainage and waste management.
He said the industrial estate requires renovation and that a cost estimate for constructing a boundary wall had been submitted to the BSCIC headquarters for allocation in the 2025–26 fiscal year.
“Once the allocation is received, steps will be taken to construct the boundary wall and resolve the other problems,” he said.
Entrepreneurs and business leaders are now questioning why basic infrastructure and service deficiencies have persisted for more than six decades despite substantial investment, production and employment at the estate.
They said timely improvements to infrastructure and services could help Dinajpur BSCIC attract new industries, retain existing businesses and create more employment opportunities.

item.title: HRW: Three laws weaken human rights safeguards in Bangladesh
item.description:
Three laws passed by parliament in September have weakened human rights protections and backtracked on reform commitments made by the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), Human Rights Watch (HRW) said Tuesday.
According to HRW, the legislation removes safeguards introduced by the interim government, which governed Bangladesh from August 2024 to February 2026, potentially weakening protections against abuses such as enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.
The interim government had introduced two ordinances aimed at strengthening the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), including by giving it powers to prevent and investigate enforced disappearances and seek accountability.
After being elected earlier this year, the government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has legislated to reduce the NHRC’s independence and investigative powers, HRW said.
The third law, the Special Response Battalion Act, formally abolishes the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) and establishes the Special Response Battalion (SRB). HRW said the law effectively renames the force while providing fewer safeguards than those applicable to regular police.
“To prevent a return to the terrible abuses of the past, Bangladesh needs real security sector reform and an independent human rights body with the authority to investigate allegations of abuse,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at HRW.
“The new government’s efforts to shield security forces from scrutiny and accountability offer no reason to trust that killings and disappearances will remain a thing of the past,” she said.
Under the Awami League government of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, which ruled Bangladesh from 2009 to 2024, law enforcement agencies committed widespread abuses, including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests of critics and excessive use of force against protesters, according to HRW.
Although killings and disappearances have declined sharply, HRW said the BNP government, like its predecessor, is holding hundreds of perceived political opponents in arbitrary detention.
The Awami League established the NHRC in 2009, but the commission lacked independence and had no authority to investigate allegations against security agencies, HRW said.
Under the previous law, a committee dominated by government or government-aligned officials selected the commissioners. When allegations were made against law enforcement agencies, the NHRC could only seek a report from the government and make recommendations.
The interim government introduced an ordinance to strengthen the commission by empowering it to investigate security agencies, creating a more independent appointments process and providing greater independence in funding and staffing.
The ordinance also established a National Preventive Mechanism to inspect and monitor places of detention, as required under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture.
However, the ordinance needed parliamentary confirmation after the February election or it would automatically lapse.
HRW said the BNP government allowed the ordinance to lapse. A new law passed on September 6, following a walkout by opposition lawmakers, does not allow the NHRC to directly investigate alleged rights violations by security forces.
Instead, the commission can request a report from the agency accused of the violation. HRW said a vaguely worded provision appears to allow the NHRC to initiate its own inquiry if the agency fails to respond or provides an unsatisfactory report.
The law also restores government control over the appointments process, reduces the commission’s budgetary and administrative independence, and weakens the status and independence of the National Preventive Mechanism.
HRW said the new law does not appear to meet the Paris Principles, the international standards for national human rights institutions, in terms of investigative powers, political independence and adequate resources.
Parliament also passed the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Act on September 6, reversing reforms introduced by an interim government ordinance, according to HRW.
While the previous ordinance empowered the NHRC to investigate allegations of enforced disappearance, the new law requires the government to appoint a security agency other than the one implicated to investigate such allegations.
The new law also removes the NHRC’s authority to monitor, inspect and investigate detention facilities, including suspected secret detention sites, HRW said.
The legal standard for command responsibility in enforced disappearance cases has also been changed.
Previously based on the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, the standard held commanders responsible for violations they should have known about and prevented. The new law requires evidence of direct orders to hold a commanding officer responsible for an enforced disappearance, according to HRW.
On September 10, parliament passed the Special Response Battalion Act, renaming RAB as the Special Response Battalion (SRB).
RAB has previously been sanctioned by the United States over allegations of serious human rights abuses. Seven former senior officers have been placed under targeted US sanctions, while several former members are facing trial at Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal over alleged crimes against humanity, including enforced disappearance.
The BNP had previously called for RAB’s dissolution.
Under the new law, RAB personnel, powers and property, including records, have been transferred to the SRB, which began operating on September 16, HRW said.
The organisation’s logo has also remained the same, with only the letters “RAB” replaced by “SRB,” according to the rights group.
In May, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said renaming the unit could lead the United States to reconsider sanctions against it.
Human rights experts have criticised the new law for what they say is a lack of safeguards, training, oversight and accountability.
HRW urged Bangladesh’s international partners to press the government to ensure that rules for the SRB include rigorous human rights vetting of personnel, independent external oversight, safeguards governing arrest and detention, preservation of RAB records and other evidence, and an end to the routine deployment of military personnel for civilian law enforcement.
The rights group also called on the United States to maintain sanctions on the renamed entity until adequate measures for human rights protection and accountability for past violations are in place.
It urged international partners, including the European Union and the United Kingdom, to express concern over what it described as the emerging human rights record and policies of the new government.
“Tarique Rahman came to office promising reform, after protesters risked their lives to overthrow a government that had committed widespread and severe rights violations,” Pearson said.
“It is deeply alarming to see the new government so quickly following in the abusive footsteps of Sheikh Hasina, because we have seen where this can lead,” she said.
